title: Regions of the vertebral column (right lateral)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: The seven vertebrae of the neck.

Small bodies; a transverse foramen in each transverse process, which carries the vertebral artery in C1 to C6; forked spinous processes in C2 to C6. The atlas (C1) has no body, the axis (C2) has the dens, and C7 has a long spinous process that can be felt.
hy: There are eight cervical spinal nerves for seven vertebrae: C1 to C7 leave above the vertebra of the same number and C8 leaves below C7.
Instability of the joint between the atlas and the dens occurs in rheumatoid arthritis and in Down syndrome and can compress the spinal cord.

rows: The twelve vertebrae of the chest. Each carries a pair of ribs.
Facets for the ribs on the bodies and on most transverse processes; heart-shaped bodies; long spinous processes that slope downward.
The five vertebrae of the lower back.
The largest bodies of the column; no rib facets and no transverse foramina; short, thick spinous processes.
hy: A lumbar puncture is done between L3 and L4 or L4 and L5, about the level of the tops of the iliac crests, below the end of the spinal cord (L1 to L2 in adults).

rows: Five fused vertebrae forming the back of the pelvis, between the two hip bones.
L5 above, the coccyx below, and the ilium on each side at the sacroiliac joint.
Sacral promontory, anterior and posterior sacral foramina, the sacral canal and the sacral hiatus.
Three to five small fused vertebrae at the lower end of the vertebral column (the tailbone).
Gives attachment to gluteus maximus, the muscles of the pelvic floor and the anococcygeal ligament.
Between the bodies of neighboring vertebrae from C2 and C3 down to L5 and S1. There is none between the atlas and the axis.
An outer ring of fibrocartilage, the anulus fibrosus, around a gel-like center, the nucleus pulposus.
Bear weight, absorb shock and allow movement between the vertebrae.
hy: In a herniated disc the nucleus pulposus bulges through the anulus, usually posterolaterally. It is most common at L4 to L5 and L5 to S1 and usually compresses the nerve root numbered for the vertebra below (L5 at an L4 to L5 disc).
The nucleus pulposus is a remnant of the notochord.
